source: ACIAR AH/2005/086 'Smallholder Cattle Best Practice Manual' (Windsor, Bush & Young), Best Practice Health and Husbandry of Cattle, Cambodia -- hosted at mekonglivestock.wordpress.com (University of Sydney / GDAHP project site)
text: Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD) is caused by a virus spread from cattle to cattle, buffalo, and pigs via direct contact, milk, faeces, urine, saliva, or indirectly on vehicles, shoes, clothing, hands, or dogs -- note that even healthy-looking animals may already be incubating and spreading it. Signs include high temperature, mouth sores with salivation, foot sores and lameness, teat sores, difficulty eating and weight loss, abortion in pregnant animals, and weight loss in calves; most cattle recover in 2-3 weeks though full weight recovery can take longer. Treatment: isolate infected animals, provide shelter and soft feed (young forage, not rice straw) plus water and rest, apply topical disinfectants/astringents (e.g. methylene blue, vinegar, lemon juice) to sores, and alert the village animal health worker -- antibiotics are not useful against the virus itself and add unnecessary cost. Prevention: vaccinate all cattle every six months, avoid all contact with sick animals (cattle and pigs), avoid contaminated material (trucks, manure, mud, feed), isolate animals during an outbreak, avoid trading or transporting cattle during an outbreak, and check any animal's disease history before purchase.
